subtitulo: The village they name instead of the country, the running-down of their own place that you are not invited to join in with, and the two comparisons that make the answer go short
cena: Ten at night on a terrace in a town you cannot pronounce, the man who poured the wine has asked where you are from, and his own answer to that question is a village forty minutes up the road.
frasePiso: You will get somebody talking about the place they are actually from. Most visitors spend a fortnight here and never get past the name of the country.
permissao: You are allowed to like it out loud while somebody is running it down in front of you — that is not contradicting anybody, that is being a guest. You are allowed to laugh at the paperwork joke: the laugh is welcome, the agreeing is not yours to do. You are allowed not to know where the town is, because asking is the entire point. And you are allowed to be the guiri and say so out loud — the joke about yourself is the one that is yours to make, and it lands every time.
espelho: Opening with 'so is it always this hot?' on the second sentence is the bit that reads as odd there — it is the same move you find tiring when somebody lands in your country and starts with the rain. Two more that travel badly in the same direction: the compliment with a comparison bolted to it, which hands somebody their own thing as a version of somebody else's; and running your own country down to be polite, which at that table reads as agreeing with the complaint rather than as modesty. The complaint was never asking for a second opinion.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You ask where she is from and she names a village of four thousand people, then stops and waits.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: She thinks I know it, or she has misheard me — I was asking which country, and she has answered something much smaller.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The first thing offered is the local one. The country is the answer with the least information in it, so it is rarely the one given first: the town, the region and sometimes the four streets around it come before it.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask '¿de qué parte?', and then ask what they eat there. Two questions, and you have the rest of the evening.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get recommendations about a real place instead of about a country, from somebody who is now telling you something they actually know.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a hotel desk in a city of four million, where 'de aquí' is the whole answer and there is no village behind it — and not abroad either, where the country goes first for them exactly as it does for you.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You say you like it here, and back comes a cheerful list of what does not work — the paperwork, the wages, the trains.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: He agrees with the bad things I had already noticed, so joining in is the friendly thing to do.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Running your own house down in front of a guest is a licence, and the licence belongs to the household. The laugh is shared; the verdict is not. A visitor who adds to the list has taken a turn that was not on offer.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Laugh, add nothing, and put one named thing of your own on the table — a market, a street, a plate.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The list stops being about a country and turns into a conversation, and you leave with the address of the place he does rate.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not when he asks you straight out what the worst of it is. That is a real question, a small specific answer is what he wanted, and hedging there reads as being managed.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You say the rice reminds you of a risotto — or that the Spanish you learned sounds nothing like his — and you get one flat syllable and a turn away.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I have offended him about Italy, or about Mexico, and I cannot tell which.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Neither, and that is why it is invisible. What lands is being handed your own thing as somebody else's version of it. A comparison leaves nothing to add, so the topic shuts; a question about where the thing comes from leaves everything to add.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Drop the comparison and ask instead: '¿hay algo típico de aquí?' Then stop talking.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get told what is actually local, at length, and usually with something put in front of you to taste.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not among themselves — the neighbours get compared all day long, in both directions, and half of that is a football table. It is the comparison arriving from outside that makes the answer go short.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You say out loud how cheap it all is, the man who served it says 'ya', and he starts wiping down the counter.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I have just paid his country a compliment about value for money, and he has not taken it.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: From where he is standing the sentence is not about what he made, it is about what his country charges. The plate, the hours behind it and the person who cooked it have all dropped out of the compliment, and what is left is a verdict on a price tag.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say the thing you actually meant: it was good, and it was worth coming for. 'Estaba buenísimo' does the whole job.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The compliment lands on the person who made it instead of on a price, and the conversation carries on past the number.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not when he says it first. 'Aquí se come bien y barato' is said with pride, and agreeing with that is agreeing with him, which is an entirely different move.

steps.pt: Part thirty-one. Warm-up: the punch. One syllable a word, and only one. PUE-blo. CÁ-ce-res. Ex-tre-ma-DU-ra.
Hand flat on your leg. Three words, three punches, and every other syllable stays the same size.
👂 'Here's the guiri!' — shouted across a bar, in the voice he uses on his own brother.

steps.promptPt: Third morning in the same bar, and the man behind the counter has just announced you to the whole room. Take the word off him and put your hand up. Speak now.
steps.es: Soy el guiri, ya lo sé.
steps.pinyin: soy el GEE-ree, yah loh SEH
steps.pt: the joke is yours to make

steps.pinyin: EHS-teh yah ehs deh lah KAH-sah
steps.pt: 'This one's one of ours now!' — that is what the joke buys, and it is instant.
Ten at night, a terrace in a town you cannot pronounce, and the man with the wine has asked where you are from.
👂 The one from part twenty-three. It is always the first thing anybody asks you.

steps.promptPt: He has poured, he has stayed at the table, and he has asked. Answer him, and hand the same thing straight back. Speak now.
steps.pt: and then it is his turn

steps.es: Yo no soy de aquí. Soy de Extremadura.
steps.pinyin: yoh noh soy deh ah-KEE. soy deh eks-treh-mah-DHOO-rah
steps.pt: 👂 'I'm not from here. I'm from Extremadura.' Second sentence out of her, and it is not the country.
steps.tts: Yo no soy de aquí. Soy de Extremadura.

steps.pt: Notice what she did not say. Not the country. She has given you a region, and then she has stopped.
The country is the least she can tell you. Everybody has one of those. Hers is a place with a name on it.
'Which part?' — three words, and it is the one that opens the whole evening.
It works after a region, after a city, after anybody at all who has told you they are from somewhere.

steps.promptPt: She has named a region and gone quiet, waiting to see whether that was enough for you. It is not. Speak now.
steps.pt: three words, and she is off

steps.es: De un pueblo cerca de Cáceres. No lo conoce nadie.
steps.pinyin: deh oon PWEH-bloh THEHR-kah deh KAH-theh-rehs. noh loh koh-NOH-theh NAH-dhyeh
steps.pt: 'A village near Cáceres. Nobody's heard of it.' — and she is smiling while she says it.
steps.tts: De un pueblo cerca de Cáceres. No lo conoce nadie.

steps.pt: That is the evening opening. Ask what they eat there and you have lost twenty minutes, in the best way.
Try it all week. Count how many towns you hear before anybody bothers to say the name of the country.
GUIRI ALERT. George here. My second sentence, every single time: 'So — is it always this hot?'
He has had that one from every single one of us, in July, at that table, all summer long.
Run it backwards. Somebody lands in Manchester and opens with the rain. You smile, and you stop listening.
Ask him about his town instead. Same effort, and he has been waiting all night for somebody to.
Now the one that catches everybody. You say you love it here, and back comes a list of what is falling apart.

steps.es: Aquí no funciona nada, ya lo verás.
steps.pinyin: ah-KEE noh foon-THYOH-nah NAH-dhah, yah loh beh-RAHS
steps.pt: 👂 'Nothing here works, you'll see.' — said cheerfully, about her own country, to a guest.
steps.tts: Aquí no funciona nada, ya lo verás.

steps.es: Es que la burocracia aquí es de risa.
steps.pinyin: ehs keh lah boo-roh-KRAH-thyah ah-KEE ehs deh RREE-sah
steps.pt: 👂 'The paperwork here is a joke.' — and he is laughing while he says it.
steps.tts: Es que la burocracia aquí es de risa.

steps.pt: That is not an invitation. It is a licence, and the licence belongs to the house.
Agree out loud and watch it go quiet for a second. Laugh with him and nothing goes quiet at all.
So laugh, and then put one thing of your own on the table. One place, with a name, that you liked.

steps.promptPt: The driver has spent ten minutes on everything that is falling down in his city. Give him back the one place he drove you past this morning — the one with the fish and the flowers. Speak now.
steps.pt: one place, named

steps.es: Bueno, el mercado sí. Eso sí.
steps.pinyin: BWEH-noh, el mehr-KAH-dhoh see. EH-soh see
steps.pt: 'Well — that, yes. That one, yes.' You have just been let off the list.
steps.tts: Bueno, el mercado sí. Eso sí.

steps.pt: The list does not stop. But you are on the other side of it now, and that is the whole of the trick.

steps.promptPt: Another night, another stool, and the man beside you has just written off the whole street you are drinking on. Do not argue with him. Tell him what you make of the few blocks around you. Speak now.
steps.pt: what you make of it, said plainly
One more, and it is the compliment that closes a topic. It is the one with a comparison inside it.
👂 One syllable, flat. It means: heard you. It also means the topic is finished.
You said the rice reminded you of a risotto. He said that, and went. Nothing rude happened at all.
It is not about the neighbours. It is about being handed your own thing as a version of somebody else's.
Same move, further away: tacos, mariachis, the big hat on the poster. That is another country, and an ocean.
If you picked yours up from an app, it very likely came from over there. Nobody here is going to correct you.
The answers just get shorter and you never find out why. So put the other question in instead.

steps.promptPt: You are one sentence away from telling him this rice is basically an Italian dish. Ask him the other thing: what belongs to this place and to nowhere else. Speak now.
steps.pt: the one question that is yours

steps.es: Uy, pues aquí lo típico es el cocido. Eso sí que hay que probarlo.
steps.pinyin: wee, pwehs ah-KEE loh TEE-pee-koh ehs el koh-THEE-dhoh. EH-soh see keh ai keh proh-BAR-loh
steps.pt: 'Ooh — what's ours here is the cocido. That you do have to try.' And now he is your guide.
steps.tts: Uy, pues aquí lo típico es el cocido. Eso sí que hay que probarlo.

steps.pt: One line to leave at home, and it sounds like praise on the way out of your mouth: 'it's so cheap here'.
Said to the man who cooked it, that is not praise for the food. It is a review of what his country costs.
Say the thing you actually meant. It was good, and it was worth coming for. You have had that since part twenty-five.
The one from the restaurant part. It is about the plate, and never about the bill.
Back to the village. When somebody names a town instead of a country, they have handed you something.
Take it. Ask which part, ask what they eat there, and the table opens up in front of you.
Not at a hotel desk in a city of four million, where 'de aquí' is the whole answer and no village is hiding.
You are allowed to like it out loud while they are running it down. That is not arguing. That is being a guest.
You are allowed to laugh at the paperwork joke. The laugh is welcome; the agreeing is not yours to do.
And you are allowed to be the guiri and say so out loud. That joke is yours, and it works every time.
The mirror: 'is it always this hot?' on the second sentence is the rain in Manchester, coming the other way.
And running your own country down to be polite reads as agreeing with the complaint. Nobody asked for that.
You will get somebody talking about the place they are actually from. Most visitors never get past the country.
Shadowing. Underneath them, out loud. Flat vowels, one punch a word, and no hurry.
Which part?
Is there something they only do here?
One more out loud, somewhere we have not stood yet, and this time nobody has asked you anything.

steps.promptPt: Last morning, the queue in a pharmacy, and the woman serving you has just said she is not from this city either. She is waiting to see whether you leave it there. Speak now.
steps.pt: and she is off again
That is it. You asked, they told you, and nobody had to speak for a whole country. Hasta luego.

aprofundar.titulo: The town, the empire and the licence to complain (optional reading)

secoes.titulo: Why the town comes before the country
secoes.corpo: Spain is a state of seventeen autonomous communities plus two cities on the North African coast, and the arrangement is not decorative: health, education, policing in some places, and the language of the street in several of them are run at that level and not from Madrid. Add to that a country where a very large number of people can still point at the village their family came from, and you get an ordinary conversational habit: the answer to 'where are you from' is normally the smallest unit the other person is likely to place, not the largest. Nothing about this is nationalism, and nobody is making a point when they do it — it is closer to the way somebody in Britain answers with the town rather than 'England'. What is different is how far down it goes and how much conversation sits on top of it: the food changes, the festival changes, the word for the same sandwich changes, and all of that is available to you the moment you ask '¿de qué parte?'. It is also why the question does more work than any compliment you could pay. A compliment ends; a question about somebody's town is a door.

exemplos.pt: deh keh PAR-teh — which part? The three words that get you the village
ee ah-YEE keh seh KOH-meh — and what do people eat there? The natural second question

secoes.titulo: The inheritance: an empire, and then a long time of being the poor south
secoes.corpo: You do not need any of this at a table, and none of it goes in your mouth — but it explains the two reactions in this part better than anything else. Spain ran one of the largest empires in history and then spent a long stretch of the modern period as the poorer, sunnier end of Western Europe: outside the industrial core, under a dictatorship until the mid-1970s, joining the European Community only in 1986, and then acquiring, in a single generation, motorways, high-speed rail and a middle class. That sequence leaves a very specific sensitivity, and it is not pride in the abstract. It is a low tolerance for being handled as the picturesque south — cheap, hot, late, a bit chaotic, lovely people. Every one of those adjectives is one a visitor deploys as a compliment. Read in that light, 'it's so cheap here' and 'is it always this hot?' stop being random irritants and become the same sentence twice. The counter-move is not to avoid the subjects; it is to talk about the specific place in front of you rather than about the country as a category.

exemplos.pt: deh behr-DAHDH — it was genuinely delicious. The compliment that lands on the person, not on the price
keh thyoo-DHAHDH mahs boh-NEE-tah — what a lovely city. About this one, not about the country

secoes.titulo: The licence to complain, and why it is not yours
secoes.corpo: Complaining about the country to a foreigner is common enough to be a genre: the paperwork, the politicians, the trains that only go to Madrid, the salaries, the summer. It is often funny, it is frequently affectionate, and it is almost never an invitation. The rule of thumb that works everywhere, not only here: the licence to run a house down belongs to the people who live in it. What the guest is offered is the laugh, not the second signature. If you want a test you can apply at speed, listen for whether the sentence ends in a full stop or in a look. 'Aquí no funciona nada' with a shrug is a bit of theatre and wants a laugh. '¿Y a ti qué te parece esto?' — asked straight, eyes up — is a real question, and there a small, specific, honest answer is exactly right, including a critical one. The failure mode is the visitor who mistakes the first for the second and starts listing. That is where the temperature drops, and it drops without anybody saying anything, which is why so many people never learn they did it.

exemplos.es: Aquí no funciona nada, ya lo verás.
exemplos.pt: 👂 nothing here works, you'll see — theatre, wants a laugh, not a verdict

exemplos.es: Pues a mí me encantó el mercado.
exemplos.pt: pwehs ah MEE meh en-kan-TOH — well, I loved the market. One named thing, and the list stops

secoes.titulo: Italy, Mexico, and the Spanish you were taught
secoes.corpo: Two comparisons come up constantly from visitors and both shorten the conversation, for the same reason and to different degrees. Italy is the neighbour: same sea, same tomatoes, same rice-and-saffron rumour, and a football-shaped rivalry that is entirely alive between themselves. Coming from a foreigner, 'this is like Italian food' is heard as being told your kitchen is a regional variant of somebody else's. Mexico is further and lands harder, because it is not a comparison at all, it is a substitution: tacos, mariachi and the wide-brimmed hat are another country on the other side of an ocean, with its own history with this one, and the visitor who arrives expecting them has effectively skipped Spain. The linguistic version is quieter and just as common: the app most people start with is largely Latin American, as is a good deal of the Spanish taught in schools in the States, so the accent you turn up with may have come from thousands of miles the other side of this country — it depends entirely on where you got it. Nobody minds and nobody will correct you — but it is worth knowing that 'the Spanish I learned sounds nothing like yours' is, from where he is standing, a slightly odd thing to announce. The reliable way out of all three is the same and it is one sentence: ask what is from here.

exemplos.pt: ai AL-goh TEE-pee-koh deh ah-KEE — is there something typical of here? The question that replaces the comparison
EHS-toh ehs deh ah-KEE — is this from here? The one-second version, said pointing at a plate

secoes.titulo: Guiri, and the one joke that is yours
secoes.corpo: 'Guiri' is what a northern European tourist gets called here. It is slang, it is usually not hostile, and it is often affectionate — the barman who uses it about you across the room is not insulting you, he is placing you, and quite often he is doing it with some warmth. There is exactly one joke about it that works in a visitor's mouth, and it is the joke about yourself: 'soy el guiri, ya lo sé' — I'm the guiri, I know. It works because it does two things at once: it shows you understood the word, and it hands the teasing back without taking it seriously. What does not work is using it about somebody else, or reaching for the affectionate insults you have just heard two friends throw at each other. That register is covered in the part before this one, and it stays receptive for a reason: mock insults between friends run on years of history you do not have yet. Yours is the self-deprecating one, and it is enough. Worth adding, because it comes up in the same breath: 'guiri' is about how you are dressed and how you are behaving as much as where you are from, and there is a version of it that costs money — shirtless two streets from the beach is a fine in several cities, and that is in the afternoon part.

exemplos.es: Soy el guiri, ya lo sé.
exemplos.pt: soy el GEE-ree, yah loh SEH — I'm the guiri, I know. The one joke about yourself
👂 this one's one of ours now — what you get back for making it
